issues.legal_issue: A statutory power to cancel a licence for repeated failures to comply with regulatory requirements, subject to an opportunity to show cause, is not an unreasonable restriction on property and business rights when its grounds are ascertainable and its exercise is directed to the statute’s public purpose.
material_facts: The statute regulated mica possession, trading and mining, and imposed requirements concerning accounts, inspections and passes.

It authorized cancellation for specified defaults, including repeated failures to comply with the statute or its rules, and required that the licensee be given the grounds and a reasonable opportunity to show cause.
The petitioner challenged the cancellation provision as an unreasonable restriction on its rights to property and to carry on business.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the cancellation provision did not impose an unreasonable restriction on the rights protected by Article 19(1)(f) and (g).
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 19(5) and (6), restrictions on the rights in Article 19(1)(f) and (g) must be reasonable. Reasonableness is assessed objectively in light of the nature of the right, the purpose and urgency of the restriction, its extent and proportionality, and prevailing conditions, as stated in State of Madras v. V. G. Row. The Court distinguished Thakur Raghubir Singh v. Court of Wards, Ajmer, where the restriction depended on unbridled executive discretion without adequate machinery. The fact that discretionary power is conferred on the State Government is only one consideration; reasonableness depends on the cumulative circumstances in which the power is conferred. The Bihar Mica Act, 1947, section 25(1)(c), provided ascertainable grounds and a hearing requirement, and served the Act’s public regulatory purpose.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_property_or_business_restriction and regulatory_scheme_serves_public_interest and cancellation_grounds_are_ascertainable and opportunity_to_show_cause_is_required

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_or_: A person challenges a law that restricts the use of property or the carrying on of a business.
predicates.regulatory_scheme_serves_public_interest: The law regulates an activity in pursuit of a public interest.
predicates.cancellation_grounds_are_ascertainable: The law specifies the kinds of defaults that may lead to cancellation.
predicates.opportunity_to_show_cause_is_required: The law requires the authority to give the affected person the grounds and an opportunity to respond before cancellation.

issues.definition: When a challenge to a property or business restriction concerns a public-interest regulatory scheme with specified cancellation grounds and a required opportunity to respond, the restriction is reasonable.

issues.legal_issue: An official exercising a quasi-judicial power to cancel a licence must not participate in the proceedings or decision when the official is personally biased against an interested person.
material_facts: The Revenue Minister was in charge of the department dealing with mines and participated in initiating the enquiry and cancelling the licence.
There was political rivalry between the Minister and a person whom the Government alleged was the real party behind the lease.
The Minister acted on the belief that the lease was held benami for that person, who was interested in the company.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the Minister was personally biased and should not have taken part in either initiating the enquiry or cancelling the licence.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to section 25(1) of the Bihar Mica Act, 1947, conferred a quasi-judicial function. The principles stated in Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh apply to authorities exercising such functions: no person may judge their own cause, and justice must manifestly appear to be done. A sufficiently substantial interest or bias disqualifies the decision-maker from participating.

predicates.quasi_judicial_licence_cancellation: An authority is deciding whether to cancel a person's licence through a proceeding requiring it to act judicially.
predicates.decision_maker_personally_biased: The decision-maker has a personal bias against a person interested in the proceeding.
predicates.decision_maker_participated: The biased decision-maker took part in initiating the proceeding or making the decision.

issues.definition: When a personally biased decision-maker participates in a quasi-judicial licence-cancellation proceeding, that decision-maker must not participate.

issues.legal_issue: A licence cannot be cancelled unless the affected person receives a reasonable opportunity to answer the case against them, assessed in light of the circumstances as a whole.
material_facts: The cancellation threatened a substantial mining interest and followed allegations concerning several mine godowns.

The company asked for particulars and later submitted a detailed explanation, but the Government retained its account books and did not allow the company to inspect them or invite further submissions.
The Government cancelled the licence after more than two years without further correspondence.
The enquiry was conducted by a department headed by a Minister who was personally biased against an interested person.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the company had not been afforded a reasonable opportunity to show cause within the meaning of the second proviso to section 25(1).
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to section 25(1) of the Bihar Mica Act, 1947, requires a reasonable opportunity to show cause before cancellation. What is reasonable depends on the circumstances and the overall picture in each case. An authority exercising a quasi-judicial function is also bound by the principles against bias stated in Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh.

rule.if: administrative_licence_cancellation and substantial_licence_interest_at_stake and response_material_withheld and decision_after_prolonged_silence and biased_official_conducted_proceeding

predicates.administrative_licence_cancellation: An authority is deciding whether to cancel a person's licence in an administrative proceeding.
predicates.substantial_licence_interest_at_stake: The licence concerns a substantial interest in carrying on the licensed activity.
predicates.response_material_withheld: The authority retains relevant records and does not let the affected person inspect them or otherwise use them to answer the allegations.
predicates.decision_after_prolonged_silence: The authority makes its decision after a prolonged period without further communication following the person's response.
predicates.biased_official_conducted_proceeding: An official personally biased against an interested person conducts or decides the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a substantial licence interest is at stake, relevant response material is withheld, the decision follows prolonged silence, and a biased official conducts the proceeding, cancellation without a reasonable opportunity to respond is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A licence cannot be cancelled for repeated non-compliance when the evidence establishes only defaults found during one continuous inspection and does not establish other repeated failures.
material_facts: The cancellation was purportedly based on repeated failures to comply with regulatory requirements.
The alleged defaults were found during inspections of different godowns over several days as part of one continuous inspection.
An earlier incident had resulted in a prosecution, but the licence was renewed for the following two years.
The record disclosed no other occasion of non-compliance, and the particulars did not establish repeated failures.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the necessary condition of repeated failure had not been established and that the Government therefore had no power to cancel the licence on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25(1)(c) of the Bihar Mica Act, 1947, made repeated failure to comply with the Act or its rules a necessary condition for cancellation. Defaults discovered in one continuous inspection did not establish repeated failure; an earlier incident followed by renewal of the licence did not establish the required pattern on this record.

rule.if: regulatory_licence_cancellation and cancellation_requires_repeated_noncompliance and alleged_defaults_found_in_one_continuous_inspection and prior_incident_followed_by_renewal and no_other_noncompliance_established

predicates.regulatory_licence_cancellation: An authority is deciding whether to cancel a licence issued under a regulatory scheme.
predicates.cancellation_requires_repeated_noncompli: The applicable cancellation ground requires repeated failures to comply with regulatory requirements.
predicates.alleged_defaults_found_in_one_continuous: The alleged defaults were found during one continuous inspection, even if it covered different sites or several days.
predicates.prior_incident_followed_by_renewal: An earlier incident was followed by renewal of the licence.
predicates.no_other_noncompliance_established: The evidence establishes no other occasion of non-compliance.

issues.definition: When cancellation requires repeated non-compliance but the alleged defaults arise from one continuous inspection, an earlier incident was followed by renewal, and no other non-compliance is established, the cancellation power is not established.
